claims.text: Standardized tensile testing can define the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility of as-cast FeNiCrMn HEA.
The resulting FeNiCrMn mechanical properties can be quantitatively compared with those of other HEAs.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is produced by arc-melting and drop-casting.
As-cast FeNiCrMn has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure with distinct grain boundaries typical of HEAs.
Dog-bone specimens should be tensile-tested at room temperature.
A tensile-test strain rate of approximately 1 × 10^-3 s^-1 is suitable.
Reproducible sample preparation will ensure a consistent FeNiCrMn microstructure.
Grain-boundary configuration, phase distribution, and dislocation density mediate the FeNiCrMn alloy's response to tensile stress.
Conventional solid-solution strengthening in FeNiCrMn gives rise to its yield strength and ductility.
Residual ordered structures formed during processing may modify the alloy's strengthening and ductility.
The proposed structural features determine the initiation and propagation of deformation.
FeNiCrMn will have measurable yield strength and ductility values in line with similar HEA systems.
FeNiCrMn will resist plastic deformation while retaining acceptable ductility.
Prior FeNiCrMn research has primarily addressed corrosion resistance, leaving its mechanical properties largely unreported.
Tensile properties have been established for the Cantor alloy and other comparison HEAs.
Small differences in processing parameters may alter the measured FeNiCrMn properties.
Ambient-temperature testing alone will not characterize behavior at other temperatures or strain rates.
Exact FeNiCrMn yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation values are uncertain because direct mechanical evidence is limited.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims that standardized tensile testing can quantify FeNiCrMn properties, but the falsification rule treats properties falling outside an analogous-HEA range as falsifying the adequacy of tensile testing. An out-of-range result would challenge the similarity prediction, not the method's ability to quantify the properties.
